stops.name: El Guetna, birth on the wadi
stops.campa: In the hamlet of El Guetna on the Wadi al-Hammam, some fifteen miles from Mascara, a son is born to Sidi Muhyi al-Din al-Hasani, shaykh of the Qadiriyya order and marabout of the tribe of the Hachem. They name him Abd al-Qadir, in honor of the Baghdad saint whose order the family has kept for generations, and trace his line through Hasan ibn Ali to the Prophet. The zawiya his father heads is at once school, court, and refuge for travelers; the boy is born into a house where scripture, arbitration, and the memory of exile from Muslim Spain are the daily furniture.

stops.name: Mascara, the zawiya school and the hafiz
stops.campa: At five he is set to reading and writing; by twelve he is permitted to comment on the Qur'an and the hadith before his father's students; by fourteen he has the whole Book by heart and is given the title hafiz. He is sent on to Oran for the higher sciences and returns to study with his cousin Mustafa ben Thami, riding and shooting as well as he construes grammar. Those who know him young remark two things at once: a scholar's stillness at the page, and a horseman's restlessness the moment he leaves it. Both will be needed.

stops.name: Mecca, the first hajj with his father
stops.campa: At seventeen he sets out with Muhyi al-Din on the road to the House of God, a journey that will run more than two years and carry him through Tunis, Cairo, Mecca, Medina, Baghdad, and Damascus. In Mecca he circles the Kaaba at his father's side and takes on the pilgrim's white cloth the first taste of a wider Islam than the wadi of his childhood: scholars from Fez and Delhi and Istanbul, all facing the one stone. He will make this circuit again as an old man, but nothing repeats the wonder of the first hajj.

stops.name: Medina, at the Prophet's tomb
stops.campa: From Mecca father and son travel north to Medina and the green-domed mosque that holds the grave of the Prophet. Abd al-Qadir prays the length of his stay beside the tomb, and here, the family tradition holds, the shape of his life to come is first impressed on him: that he is marked for a labor larger than the zawiya, though neither he nor his father yet gives it a name. He lingers at the Rawda, the garden between pulpit and tomb that the Prophet himself called a garden of Paradise.

stops.name: Baghdad, at the grave of Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani
stops.campa: The pilgrimage bends east to Baghdad, to the shrine at Bab al-Sheikh where the founder of the Qadiriyya order lies, the saint after whom the boy himself is named. He kneels at the tomb of Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani and renews in his own person the six-centuries-old chain of the order his father heads in Algeria — teacher to teacher, unbroken, back to this grave. He will carry the order's discipline, its silence and its patience under blows, into a war no one here yet foresees.

stops.name: Damascus, at the tomb of Ibn Arabi
stops.campa: On the slope of Mount Qasiyun, in the Salihiyya quarter, the young pilgrim prays at the grave of Muhyi al-Din Ibn Arabi, the Andalusian mystic dead five hundred and eighty-six years, whom the Sufis call al-Shaykh al-Akbar, the Greatest Master. He is eighteen. He does not know, and no one tells him, that he will die an old man a street's width from this stone and be laid beside it; that the book he will one day write, the Kitab al-Mawaqif, will be a lifelong commentary poured out at this master's feet. He leaves Damascus marked, though the mark has no name yet either.
stops.quote: He is our treasure, from which we draw what we write.
stops.quote_source: Kitab al-Mawaqif, on Ibn Arabi (composed later in Damascus)

stops.name: Mascara, return and marriage
stops.campa: After a second circuit of the Kaaba the pair turn home, more than two years and several thousand miles behind them. Abd al-Qadir marries his cousin Kheira bint Boutaleb the same year and settles, for a season, into the life the zawiya expects of a shaykh's son: teaching, arbitration, the discipline of the order. Three years later French guns will land at Sidi Fredj, and the season of study closes for good.

stops.name: Plain of Eghris, near Mascara — proclaimed Amir al-Mu'minin
stops.campa: Two years into the French landing, with Oran province ungoverned and burning, the elders of the Hachem, Beni Amer, and Gharaba tribes gather on the plain of Eghris under a great elm. Muhyi al-Din, too old for the saddle, has already refused the emirate for himself; he puts forward his son. Abd al-Qadir, twenty-four, is seated beneath the tree; his father swears the oath of allegiance first, then the notables one by one. He accepts the title Nasir al-Din, Defender of the Faith, and the acclaim: Amir al-Mu'minin, Commander of the Believers. Five days later the oath is renewed at the great mosque of Mascara before the assembled town.

stops.name: Mascara, the Treaty of Desmichels
stops.campa: Fifteen months into the war the French general Desmichels, worn down by raids he cannot end, signs with the young emir a treaty that concedes him sovereignty over the interior of Oran province, holding only the coastal towns himself. Abd al-Qadir reads it as recognition of a state; Paris will read it, once the ink dries, as a temporary truce with a bandit. He uses the peace as his father used the zawiya: to build. Within three years he governs, by treaty and by the sword, a country the size of a European kingdom.

stops.name: La Macta, the marsh victory
stops.campa: General Trézel marches a column toward Mascara and is caught retreating through the reed-marsh of the Macta river; the emir's cavalry breaks it there, in the mud, with heavy French dead and the abandonment of guns and baggage. It is the first outright disaster France suffers in Algeria and it makes Abd al-Qadir's name ring from Algiers to the Chamber of Deputies in Paris: not a raider to be bought off, but a general. The victory buys him two more years to build his state before Bugeaud's heavier hand closes on him.

stops.name: Mascara and Tlemcen, the towns fall
stops.campa: In December Marshal Clauzel storms and burns Mascara, the emir's own town, forcing him to move his government to the new capital he is raising at Tagdemt; in January Tlemcen falls in its turn. He does not fight to hold cities he cannot hold; the war he wages is fought in open country, on his own terms, with the tribes as his infantry and distance as his fortress. Losing the towns does not lose him the war — it only proves what kind of war it is.

stops.name: Oued Sikkak, defeat before Bugeaud
stops.campa: Thomas Robert Bugeaud, newly arrived and newly ferocious, meets the emir's army on the Sikkak river near Tlemcen and breaks it in open battle, the first clear French field victory of the war. Abd al-Qadir withdraws in good order; he has learned, as he will keep learning, that no pitched battle against French artillery can be won and that the war must be fought as raid, siege, and negotiation, never as a single day's gamble.
